narrative:
The model estimated a 69.3% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That does not mean failure is certain, but it means the model judged failure more likely than success, and your application was rejected on that high-risk basis.

The strongest reason was your third-year class standing. You were in the lowest decile of your class in year three (1.00), while accepted students averaged much higher (5.79). This factor pushed most strongly toward predicted bar failure. The second strongest factor was your first-year class standing: again lowest decile (1.00) versus an average of 6.00 among accepted students, also pushing toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential factor. At 3.00 it was below the accepted-student average of 3.23, but it was the one top factor that pushed toward passing, slightly softening rather than worsening the prediction.

To move forward, ask the admissions office whether you can appeal, explain any exceptional circumstances, or reapply with new evidence. Consider strengthening your academic record through additional coursework, seek bar-exam readiness support, and discuss whether retaking the LSAT or obtaining admissions counseling would improve a future application. Apply to a balanced range of schools and ask what specific updates would be considered. Use this as a risk signal to address, not a final judgment of your ability.
